Convatec (CTEC-GB): a reliable compounder of 13 to 14 percent a year on a bottom-quartile multiple, where the next year's return depends on worries clearing, not on estimate upgrades

Investment memo, 18 Nov 2026, the day of Convatec's ten-month trading update. Figures are in US dollars on the company's adjusted basis unless stated; share prices and per-share values are in pence. The memo uses a share price of 268p, after today's rise of about 9 percent (end note A1).

The case in four sentences. Convatec is a good, non-cyclical business that is delivering what it promised, and its shares trade on a multiple still in the bottom quarter of their ten-year range. Convatec's earnings should compound at 13 to 14 percent a year to 2030, and that earnings path is reliable to 2027. Because consensus already sits on the same earnings path, any extra return must come from the multiple recovering as a stack of worries clears one by one. Those worries are clearing on a dated calendar that is favourable until about August 2027 and then turns on one external decision: the Medicare payment amounts due in late summer 2027.
14.2xTwo-year-forward P/E at 268p, about the 20th percentile of ten years
16x / 17.34xMy central end-2027 multiple, and the guideline fair multiple
13 to 14%EPS growth a year to 2030, on 6 percent revenue growth
+32%Central total return to end-2027 at 16 times (+42% at the guideline)
about 16% a yearReturn to mid-2029 even if the multiple stays at 14.2 times

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The business. Convatec sells recurring consumables for chronic conditions in four franchises: Advanced Wound Care (31 percent of revenue), Ostomy (28 percent), Continence (22 percent, including the US home-delivery distributor 180 Medical) and Infusion sets (19 percent). Over 90 percent of Convatec's revenue recurs. The company reports in dollars, and its shares trade in pence.

The investment case in five steps

1
Delivery is proven. Today's update showed the promised growth acceleration: organic growth excluding InnovaMatrix of 6.6 percent for ten months, which implies about 9 percent in July to October (#2).
↓
2
There is no estimate gap to close. Guidance, consensus and my forecasts sit on the same line, so delivery alone lifts FY2027 consensus EPS by only 1 to 2 percent (#6, #7).
↓
3
Worries, not earnings, hold the multiple down. At 14.2 times, Convatec trades in the bottom quarter of its ten-year range. Three of the worries have cleared; the two that matter most, the margin print on 23 Feb 2027 and the Medicare payment amounts in late summer 2027, are open but dated (#10).
↓
4
Re-rating drives the 13-month return. My central end-2027 multiple is 16 times, against a guideline of 17.34 times; the multiple supplies about half of the 13-month return at the guideline (#11, #12).
↓
5
Compounding drives the three-year return. To mid-2029 earnings supply most of the return: about 16 percent a year at an unchanged multiple, and about nil rather than a loss at a trough multiple with an earnings miss (#12).

Seven insights

1 · The key messageToday's update was a re-rating event, not an upgrade event. Convatec raised its organic growth guidance, but dollar revenue, operating profit and EPS did not rise, because currency took back what growth added. Since the September low the shares have risen about 23 percent, while consensus FY2027 EPS has risen only about 1 percent.
2 · MarginConvatec's underlying margin is expanding about three times faster than its reported margin. The FY2026 margin floor of 23.0 percent implies a reported rise of 70 basis points, but a rise of about 225 basis points before currency and the loss of InnovaMatrix. Holding the floor while absorbing 35 basis points more headwind since August is a guidance raise in everything but name (#4).
3 · Track recordConvatec's margin record is better than the earlier research answers concluded. In constant currency the company beat its opening margin floor by 70 to 110 basis points in three of the last four years and raised the floor during the year twice. In the years when the reported margin fell short, currency was the cause (#4).
4 · GrowthConvatec's growth acceleration is real but narrow. On my arithmetic, Infusion grew roughly 20 to 24 percent in July to October and supplied about half of the group's growth from a fifth of the group's revenue (#2).
5 · PhasingConvatec's 2027 will be two unequal halves. The first half of 2027 laps a depressed first half of 2026: revenue up about 7.4 percent, margin up about 180 basis points and EPS up 20 to 25 percent. The second half laps today's surge, and EPS rises only about 7 percent. Nothing in the business changes between the two halves (#6).
6 · ExpectationsEstimate upgrades will be small, but the improvement in the reported story can be large. I expect FY2027 consensus EPS to rise about 1 to 2 percent over twelve months. Over the same period, reported organic growth rises from about 4 percent to about 6.5 percent, reported EPS roughly doubles as the spin-out amortisation ends, and the first half of 2027 prints the best year-on-year comparisons in years (#7).
7 · ReturnTime shifts the source of the return from the multiple to earnings. To the end of 2027, about half of the return at the guideline multiple comes from re-rating. To mid-2029 most of the return comes from earnings, and at an unchanged multiple the return is still about 16 percent a year. Even at a trough multiple with an earnings miss, the three-year return is about nil rather than a loss (#12).

Where I differ from the market

The sell-side reads today's update as "execution delivered" and as the start of a re-rating towards peers, and applies multiples of 14.5 to 18 times to reach targets of 280p to 315p. I agree with the direction. I differ from the sell-side in five places:

(i) Margin
I see more hidden strength in Convatec's margin than brokers' notes do (#4).
(ii) Buybacks
I see less EPS gain from buybacks, about 1.5 percent a year net of interest rather than the gross figure quoted, and I expect the next buyback in August 2027, not February (#5).
(iii) Breadth
Brokers describe the acceleration as broad-based; I find that it came mostly from Infusion (#2).
(iv) Phasing
No broker yet frames Convatec's 2027 as two unequal halves (#6).
(v) Europe
The German and French price measures are under-discussed for Convatec specifically (#1).

#1Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Conclusion on #1The operating environment gives Convatec steady demand but no tailwind to growth. Its headwinds are real but dated, sized, mostly in the forecasts and slowly easing, so the environment constrains the investment case without threatening it.

Evidence. Demand for Convatec's products is structural and visible, but it adds nothing to the acceleration: Convatec's markets grow 4 to 5 percent a year, and customers reorder for years. Three external forces act on Convatec's prices and costs, and each force has a date:

From 1 Jan 2028
US Medicare competitive bidding. About 7 percent of group revenue is billed to Medicare by 180 Medical, and about 2 percent more goes through distributors that depend on Medicare. Retail prices under bidding are expected to fall 20 to 30 percent.
From 2027
European reimbursement cuts. Germany cuts reimbursement by about 3 percent and is tightening the evidence it requires for wound dressings. France's draft budget carries a 3.6 percent levy on reimbursed devices, worth about €10.8m or 2.1 percent of Convatec's pre-tax profit on Jefferies' figures, about four times the sector average. The French parliament rejected the draft budget; the final law is due in late December 2026.
2027
Input costs, as the 12-month hedges roll off. Each point of input inflation above the planned 3 percent costs Convatec $7m to $8m in 2027.

Competition adds a fourth force: Coloplast is putting about 80 percent of its DKK 500m of savings into US chronic care.

Since September 2026 the direction of these forces has improved on five counts:

  • A bipartisan bill introduced on 9 Oct 2026 would keep ostomy and continence products out of Medicare bidding for five years.
  • The final bidding rule is softer than earlier rounds: Medicare will pay at the 75th percentile of winning bids, and suppliers must furnish the brand that the physician prescribes.
  • On today's call management put 2027 input inflation at 3 to 4 percent (AlphaSense's summary of the call), against the chief executive's remark in August that input inflation would "double".
  • Oil is back below $100 a barrel.
  • Coloplast has reset its targets to 5 to 7 percent growth with a flat margin and neutral-to-negative pricing, which is a rational rival lowering its own bar.

Inference. The external environment does not help Convatec grow; it sets the size of a tax on Convatec's earnings. If every external measure lands, the tax is roughly 1 to 2 points of revenue and 50 to 150 basis points of margin across 2027 and 2028.

For a share on a bottom-quartile multiple, the trend in the worries matters more than their level, and that trend is improving. On Medicare bidding the surprise is one-sided, because the forecasts already assume that bidding proceeds: a deferral (about three chances in ten) adds to earnings, and a base-case outcome subtracts nothing.

So what. Treat the external environment as three dated scenarios, not as a mood. The most valuable external date is late summer 2027, when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) publishes the bidding payment amounts: the publication turns an open-ended fear into a number that the market can model and absorb.

The strongest counter-case. The payer has form. One CMS rule cut the price of InnovaMatrix by 85 percent and removed $64m of Convatec's revenue in a year. Private insurers tend to index their prices to Medicare's. A second bidding round is likely around 2031. The 2008 precedent for a bidding delay was paid for with a 9.5 percent cut to the fee schedule, so a deferral would be relief, not an all-clear. And the sector's valuation remains exposed to bond yields near 5 percent.

What would change my view. Negatively: a CMS proposal that touches another chronic-care category; payment amounts implying a price cut of 30 percent or more; the French levy enacted as drafted, with Germany going further; polymer prices feeding through at 6 percent or more. Positively: committee action on the bipartisan bill, or payment amounts implying a cut nearer 20 percent.

Against the market. I agree with brokers that Medicare bidding is the main overhang and is only partly in FY2028 estimates. I differ on two points: no broker note I have seen sizes the European measures for Convatec, and the 2027 input-inflation risk now looks smaller than notes written before today assume.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. Demand is structural, non-discretionary and grows 4 to 5 percent, but it adds nothing to the acceleration, while dated external threats take an estimated 1 to 2 points of revenue and 50 to 150bp of margin across 2027-28: Medicare bidding from 2028 on about 9 percent of revenue, German and French reimbursement cuts, hedge roll-off on inputs and Coloplast's US counter-investment. The trend is improving (the bipartisan bill, a softer final rule, inflation guided at 3 to 4 percent, a rival lowering its own bar), so this is a mild net headwind in the mid-40s, in line with the group's 40 but a little above it for the improvement; better than Carlsberg's mature beer and below Kerry's neutral balance.

#2Internally-driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

Conclusion on #2Convatec's internal change forces are strong, broad and funded, and today's update showed them in the growth line. Their weaknesses are a dependence on Infusion, a thin leadership bench during the heaviest launch year, and cash flow that lags earnings.

Evidence. Today's update supplied the proof of acceleration that the market had awaited since May 2026. Organic growth excluding InnovaMatrix was 6.6 percent for the ten months to October, against 5.0 percent at the half-year, which implies about 9 percent in July to October. Four engines drive the change:

Products. The first wave of launches supplied over half of first-half growth. Esteem Body has reached about $60m a year and about 15 percent of its US segment within two years. ConvaFoam has lifted its share of foam dressings from 5 to about 6 percent, and each point of share is worth about $23m. GentleCath Air for Women doubled its sales. In 2027 come Natura Body in the US (mid-year, aimed at the 60 to 65 percent of the US ostomy market that uses two-piece soft convex products), full US launches of ConvaVac and ConvaFiber, and the diabetic-foot-ulcer trial results for ConvaNiox.
Infusion. Convatec makes about two-thirds of the world's infusion sets and is the sole supplier of sets to all three subcutaneous Parkinson's therapies. Customers forecast their orders a year ahead. Capacity, not demand, has set Infusion's pace, and new automated capacity arrives in 2027 under customers' minimum volume commitments.
Cost. General and administrative cost has fallen from 13 to about 6 percent of sales, and the number of plants from nine to five. Packaging automation completes in 2027.
Capital. Convatec bought back $500m of shares in 2025 and 2026 under a policy of holding leverage at 2.0 times EBITDA.

How narrow was the acceleration?

Infusion supplied about half of the group's July to October growth, on my arithmetic. The company discloses segment growth only in bands, so the segment figures are derived. Weighting the segments by last year's revenue, a group growth rate of about 9 percent in July to October requires Infusion growth of roughly 20 to 24 percent in those four months.

Morgan Stanley's back-solved segment figures, as AlphaSense relays them, point to broader growth but do not reconcile with the group figure. The figures (Infusion 13.9 percent, Continence 7.4, Ostomy 6.1, Advanced Wound Care 3.7) combine to group growth of only about 7.3 percent; they match the group figure only if 13.9 percent is Infusion's ten-month rate.

Whether Ostomy accelerated is the open question. If Morgan Stanley's Ostomy figure is right, Ostomy accelerated from 4.3 to about 6 percent, which the company's wording ("mid single digit, similar to H1") would hide, and the acceleration would be broader than the earlier research answers concluded. The segment table in the FY2026 results on 23 Feb 2027 will settle the question. Advanced Wound Care did not accelerate on either reading.

The problems: new leaders, a warning letter and lagging cash. The leaders who must deliver the next step are new or missing: a chief executive in the role for a year, a chief financial officer who starts on 1 Mar 2027, a head of research lost to Insulet in June 2026, and a head of operations still being recruited. The Reynosa infusion plant is under a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) warning letter, with remediation running through 2027. Management says the letter does not concern patient safety or product quality; the earlier research answers found that the letter cites leak-test validation and adverse-event reporting, which is more serious in kind, although the practical consequences for the plant are unchanged. Cash is running behind earnings: today Convatec cut its equity cash conversion to about 90 percent, and leverage will end 2026 nearer 2.1 than 2.0 times. A third of shareholders voted against the 2026 remuneration report.

Inference. The four engines are largely independent of each other, which lowers the chance that they fail together: cost savings do not need launches to succeed, and buybacks need only EBITDA and cash. But the engines belong to the second act of a programme that began in 2019, so they sustain 13 to 14 percent EPS growth rather than create a step-up against expectations. And growth now leans on one franchise, Infusion, more than the breadth of the past record suggests.

So what. Give high confidence to cost savings and capital returns, and medium confidence to launches and Infusion. Watch two things that the headline growth figure will not show: whether Ostomy really accelerated, and whether the new Infusion capacity is validated on time at a plant under an FDA warning letter.

The strongest counter-case. A former Convatec research director expects the move to central control to slow launches and cost the company people. Eight launches are landing on a sales force and a research organisation that have just lost leaders. Tandem's tubeless pump contains no Convatec components, and the long-run shift to patch pumps threatens the franchise that carries the growth.

What would change my view. A slipped date for Natura Body or for the new Infusion line; any escalation of the FDA warning letter; a further senior departure; Infusion orders that reverse in the first half of 2027.

Against the market. Brokers call the acceleration broad-based. I think the acceleration is led by Infusion, with a possible but unconfirmed contribution from Ostomy. I agree with brokers that today's update lifts management's credibility.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. A clear, funded, multi-part programme now visible in the growth line: organic growth excluding InnovaMatrix raised to 6.6 percent for ten months (about 9 percent in July to October), launches supplying over half of growth, contracted Infusion capacity arriving in 2027, overhead cut from 13 to about 6 percent of sales with about 225bp of underlying margin expansion in FY2026, and systematic buybacks; the operating margin is up 5.1 points over three years (78.5th percentile). Held below the mid-70s because it is the second act of a 2019 programme that sustains rather than steps up earnings, growth leans on Infusion, and the leadership bench is thin during the heaviest launch year, with Infusion capacity remediating under an FDA letter and cash conversion cut; slightly above the group's 68 for the proof delivered today, just below Theon and above OEM International.

#3Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Conclusion on #3A favourable industry structure, two genuine moats and a reliable management team make Convatec an above-average business. Three things hold Convatec below top quality: its challenger position in its largest markets, its lack of pricing power and its exposure to the payer.

Evidence.

Structure. About 70 percent of Convatec's revenue sits in concentrated, sticky oligopolies. The top three companies hold over three-quarters of the ostomy market and about 69 percent of continence, and infusion sets are a near monopoly. Rivals compete on clinical evidence and service, not on list price, and new entrants have taken almost no share in Western markets in five years. The other 30 percent of revenue, wound care, is fragmented and driven by procurement.
Position. Convatec leads only in infusion sets and in US catheter home delivery, where 180 Medical has about 40 percent share and customer churn under 1 percent. Convatec is number three in ostomy, 20 to 40 share points behind Coloplast, and number four in wound care.
Moats. Two of Convatec's moats are hard and widening: infusion sets written into partners' regulatory filings, and a captive US channel (180 Medical) that earns both the manufacturer's and the retailer's margin. The other moats (nurse-led switching costs, adhesives know-how and regulatory barriers) are shared with stronger incumbents.
Financial profile. Convatec's gross margin of about 60 percent is seven points below Coloplast's. Return on invested capital is 13 to 16 percent, up from 7 percent in 2019. Free cash flow has been about 0.8 times adjusted net income and will be about 0.5 times in FY2026, as capital spending peaks at about 9 percent of sales. Leverage of 2.0 to 2.1 times is a deliberate choice.

Against peers. Consensus expects Convatec's EPS to grow faster than Coloplast's and Smith & Nephew's in each of the next three years (chart below), and Convatec's EBITDA margin to rise from 26 to 29 percent while Coloplast's stays flat at 30 percent.

Management. Convatec's management team is reliable: it executes what it announces within months, holds one outlier standard (overhead cost), targets growth above the market leader's and returns surplus cash systematically. The team is not an outlier on innovation, quality systems or capital allocation: $141m of the roughly $500m spent on acquisitions since 2021 has been written off.

Inference. Convatec's industry structure is among the better ones in European healthcare, and it explains the stable margins and low churn. The structure is robust against competitors but fragile against one actor, the payer.

Vertical integration gives Convatec direct access to the patient and a second margin, and for the same reason places more of its profit where payers act first: 7 percent of Convatec's revenue is billed directly to Medicare, against about 1 percent of Coloplast's. The quality gap to Coloplast is closing from both ends, because Convatec is improving while the market leader resets.

7%Convatec revenue billed directly to Medicare
about 1%Coloplast revenue billed directly to Medicare

So what. Convatec is a medium-to-high quality franchise, not a high-return compounder. The franchise supports a mid-to-high-teens multiple when it is delivering, which is where the shares traded for most of 2019 to 2024, not the 30 times that Coloplast once earned.

The strongest counter-case. Convatec has never shown Coloplast's consistency over a full cycle. In ostomy, the largest prize, the pull of the installed base favours Coloplast and Hollister, and Coloplast now has about $60m a year to spend on the same US hospital accounts. With no pricing power, Convatec must meet any cost shock with productivity.

What would change my view. Share losses at hospital discharge in US ostomy; a second quality failure; a large acquisition; evidence that 180 Medical's volume gains do not offset the 2028 Medicare price cut.

Against the market. I agree with consensus that the quality gap to Coloplast has narrowed. I add two points: the pair trade (long Convatec, short Coloplast) is now the consensus trade, and that trade underweights Convatec's greater exposure to both of the next two payer measures, Medicare bidding and the European reimbursement cuts.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. About 70 percent of revenue sits in concentrated, sticky oligopolies with two hard, widening moats (sets written into partners' filings, the captive 180 Medical channel with churn under 1 percent) and over 90 percent recurring, non-cyclical revenue, run by a reliable cost-disciplined team; but it is a number-three challenger in ostomy and number four in fragmented wound care, has no pricing power and is fragile against one actor, the payer. Adjusted ROIC of 13 to 16 percent (the reported 5.9 percent, 43.6th percentile, is goodwill-distorted) and a 78th-percentile gross margin show an above-average profile, while new capital is mixed: contracted Infusion capacity earns well but $141m of about $500m of acquisitions was written off; coherent with the groups (60, 47, 60, 63), just below Carlsberg and above Helios Towers.

#4Conservatism of guidance, management of expectations, and the track record

Conclusion on #4Convatec's guidance is conservative on margin and on growth within the year, and its delivery record is better in constant currency than it looks as reported. Management keeps consensus at the floor of guidance, although the cushion in growth guidance is now thinner than its history implies.

Evidence: the margin record, restated. The earlier research answers disagreed on Convatec's margin record: one set saw a miss in FY2022, and another saw floors met but never beaten. The AlphaSense report on the guidance record, which cites the company's own documents, supports neither reading:

In constant currency the company beat its opening margin floor by 70 to 110 basis points in three of four years, and raised the floor during the year twice, through cost inflation of 8.6 percent in 2022 and 6.5 percent in 2023. In the years when the reported margin undershot (2023 and 2024), currency cost about 60 basis points. The AlphaSense report labels the basis of its figures inconsistently in places and gives two dates for the 2023 raise, so I rate the restated record medium confidence and would have it verified.

Evidence: the hidden raise in FY2026. Convatec is holding its FY2026 margin floor of at least 23.0 percent on a reported basis, and holding that floor requires about 225 basis points of underlying expansion:

Evidence: growth guidance. Convatec has raised or narrowed its in-year growth guidance upwards in most years, always at the half-year or the ten-month update. But the cushion has shrunk as the bar has risen: delivery beat the initial guidance midpoint by 0.85 to 1.95 points in 2020 to 2024, and by only 0.4 and about 0.7 points in 2025 and 2026. The midpoint of the mid-term growth range of 6 to 8 percent is above anything Convatec delivered in the last two years.

Evidence: expectations management. Management actively holds expectations at the floor. It names the low end of its 2027 margin range (24 percent), quantifies each headwind in basis points, cut InnovaMatrix guidance twice ahead of the numbers, calls EPS growth "double-digit" when consensus has 14 percent, and today flagged lower cash conversion and higher capital spending alongside the growth raise. As a result, consensus sits on the floor of guidance.

Inference. Convatec's margin guidance is conservative in the way that counts: the company sets the opening floor where it can absorb a shock and still land on it. Growth guidance is conservative within the year, because November and December need only about 4.5 percent growth to reach the bottom of the new range, but it is no longer conservative at the mid-term midpoint.

So what. FY2027 guidance on 23 Feb 2027 will most likely restate the mid-term targets: 6 to 8 percent organic growth, a margin of at least 24.0 percent and double-digit EPS growth. Because the InnovaMatrix headwind does not recur in 2027, the 24.0 percent floor needs only about 100 basis points of expansion, in a year after the underlying engine delivered more than twice that. The margin cushion is real; whether it shows as a margin beat or is spent on launches is management's choice.

The strongest counter-case. FY2025 landed mid-range, only 20 basis points above the bottom of guidance. The chief executive said today that "we are investing to accelerate growth", and Coloplast has just chosen a flat margin to fund growth, so Convatec's surplus margin is more likely to be spent than to drop through. The reported margin is what drives EPS, and currency has been a margin headwind in three of the last four years. A new chief financial officer will set her first bar low.

What would change my view. An FY2026 margin below 23.0 percent; an FY2027 margin floor below 24.0 percent; an FY2027 growth range below 6 to 8 percent.

Against the market. Morgan Stanley notes that margin guidance "was not raised in proportion" to growth guidance. I read the same fact the other way: the margin floor did not move while the headwinds grew, so the underlying bar rose.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. In constant currency the opening margin floor was beaten by 70 to 110bp in three of four years and raised in-year twice, growth guidance has been raised or narrowed upwards in most years (again today), and management actively holds consensus at the floor; the FY2026 floor is held while absorbing 35bp more headwind, a hidden raise. Held below 70 because the reported margin undershot on currency, FY2025 landed only mid-range, InnovaMatrix guidance was cut twice, cash conversion was cut today, the growth cushion has thinned and the mid-term midpoint is above recent delivery, with the record itself only of medium confidence; above the groups' 60 and 50 for the constant-currency record, just below Odfjell Drilling and above MITIE.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Conclusion on #5Convatec's business model turns 6 percent revenue growth into 13 percent EPS growth through moderate operating leverage, half-absorbed cost savings and a mechanical buyback, with no help from price.

Evidence. The forecasts convert revenue growth into EPS growth in four steps (average growth a year, FY2025 to FY2030):

Pricing power: absent. Convatec's like-for-like price is about plus 0.3 points now, slightly negative in 2027 and about minus 1.5 points in 2028. Convatec's only price lever is mix from premium launches, worth 1 to 1.5 points of growth inside volume.
Operating leverage: moderate. Convatec's contribution margin is about 75 percent, but the incremental margin actually delivered is 30 to 40 percent (38, 40, 30, 32 and 31 percent across FY2026 to FY2030 in the forecasts), because management reinvests about half of the gain.
Cost-out: real, but mostly absorbed. Gross cost savings of 100 to 130 basis points a year are available to 2028, but only 40 to 60 basis points reach the margin after inflation, depreciation on new production lines and launch spending.
Financial leverage: mechanical. Each $100m of buyback retires about 1.5 percent of the shares and costs about 0.9 percent of net income in interest, so each $100m adds about 0.6 percent to EPS. Across the buyback programme, the net gain is about 1.5 percent of EPS a year.

Feedback loops.

Three loops reinforce growth: Infusion (specification in partners' filings, then contracted capacity), launches (clinical evidence, then adoption, share and funding for research) and the leverage-buyback loop.
Four loops balance it: payer price resets, Coloplast's counter-investment, purchasing-group concessions that grow with volume, and the lag between input prices and hedges.

Inference. Six percent revenue growth becomes 13 percent EPS growth, a multiplier of about 2.2 times. About a third of the gap between the two growth rates comes from the business (operating leverage and cost savings), and about half comes from the balance sheet. The mix is shifting from self-help margin gains, which the market discounts as execution risk, towards revenue growth and mechanical capital return, which the market tends to trust more.

So what. The reliable part of Convatec's above-average profit growth is the buyback loop, which is wholly in management's hands. The part with upside is operating leverage in 2027, when the underlying margin engine (#4) meets a year without the InnovaMatrix drag.

The strongest counter-case. Convatec's margin expansion is running at half the pace of 2021 to 2025, and the industry's own precedent is that margins settle in the mid-20s, where Coloplast's stopped. Without pricing power, a cost shock larger than productivity gains lands on the margin in full. Buyback accretion depends on the multiple staying low; at 17 times, the accretion roughly halves.

What would change my view. Evidence of like-for-like price rises above inflation (unlikely); a gross margin that rises before 2028; or, negatively, incremental margins below 30 percent in 2027.

Against the market. The market narrative credits buybacks with a "10 percent EPS tailwind over three years", which is gross of interest. Net of interest, I have about 4 percent by FY2029 against consensus. I agree with the market that Infusion's growing share of the mix lifts the group margin, although nobody can audit that claim without segment profit disclosure.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. The structure holds real operating gearing (a contribution margin of about 75 percent, so most of the cost base is fixed), real cost-out (100 to 130bp a year gross to 2028) and a mechanical buyback adding about 1.5 percent a year net of interest, turning 6 percent revenue growth into about 13 percent EPS growth, a 2.2 times multiplier against about 2 times for the median. It is held near the 60s rather than 75 because there is no pricing power (like-for-like price turning negative in 2027-28 under payer resets), delivered incremental margins are only 30 to 40 percent as half the gain is reinvested, and balancing loops (payer resets, purchasing-group concessions, Coloplast's counter-investment) offset the reinforcing ones; slightly above the groups' 60 and 57 for the fixed-cost share in a non-cyclical business where gearing is unlikely to bite in reverse.

#6Forecast financials, and the scope for double-digit growth

Conclusion on #6The forecasts show reliable double-digit EPS growth of 13 to 14 percent a year on 6 percent revenue growth, with faster revenue and cash growth than in the past and slower margin gains. The forecasts sit on consensus until Medicare bidding separates them in FY2028.

Evidence. The forecasts of record use the model's lines down to net income, and EPS on the Analyst's share-count path (end note A2):

Compared with the last four to six years, the forecasts have revenue growing faster (6.1 percent a year, against 4.9 to 5.6 percent), the margin climbing at half the pace (about 58 basis points a year, against 115), EPS growing at about the same rate, and free cash flow more than doubling as capital spending falls from about 9 to about 5.6 percent of sales.

By half-year, the forecasts need revenue of about $1,322m at a margin of about 24.6 percent in the second half of 2026, about $1,323m at 23.0 percent in the first half of 2027, and about $1,394m at 25.0 percent in the second half of 2027.

Against consensus, the totals agree but the parts do not. For FY2028 I have operating profit 2 percent lower than consensus, interest of $86m against consensus's figure of about $59m (consensus quietly deleverages, which contradicts Convatec's stated leverage policy), net income 6 percent lower and about 4.5 percent fewer shares, which brings EPS back to within 2 percent of consensus. By segment, consensus looks too high in Advanced Wound Care ($788m of FY2027 revenue, against $757m in the forecasts) and too low in Infusion.

Inference. Double-digit EPS growth is well supported for five years, and FY2026 and FY2027 rest on things the company has already shown. Two years break the line: FY2026 on revenue (the InnovaMatrix hole) and FY2028 on Medicare bidding. Growth above the past rate is plausible in revenue and cash, but not in margin.

So what. The forecasts equal consensus to FY2027. The differentiated views are the composition of earnings (less operating profit, more buyback), FY2028 (Medicare bidding) and the phasing inside 2027. One caution on optics: the forecasts assume flat exchange rates. The dollar has strengthened since the first half of 2026, so reported growth in the first half of 2027 will trail organic growth, as reported growth did today. For a sterling-based holder, the same currency move adds to EPS in pence.

The strongest counter-case. The base case assumes the lower half of the growth range and the bottom of the margin range, and both can still be missed: if wound care stays at 3 to 4 percent growth and Infusion slows against its comparatives, 2027 group growth is 5.5 percent and EPS about 21.8 cents. Free cash flow in FY2026 also needs a second-half working-capital release near the top of the five-year range.

What would change my view. Segment disclosure on 23 Feb 2027 showing Ostomy growth of 6 percent or more (positive) or Infusion orders pulled forward from 2027 (negative); the 2027 hedge cover and input-inflation assumption.

Against the market. The forecasts are in line with consensus EPS for FY2026 and FY2027, about 2 percent below consensus for FY2028 and level with consensus for FY2029.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. About 13 percent sits in the 10 to 15 percent B band, honest and on consensus to FY2027, against consensus growth at the 54th percentile. Placed a little above mid-band because the growth is organic rather than bought, revenue grows faster than the past (6.1 against 4.9 to 5.6 percent) and the margin climbs from 22.3 to 25.2 percent, above any past year, but held from the upper band because the margin rises at half the past pace and about 4 of the 13 points come from a falling share count.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Conclusion on #7Scope for estimate upgrades is modest and slightly positive, scope for the narrative to improve is considerable and largely mechanical, and both are front-loaded into the nine months to August 2027.

Evidence and probabilities (the probabilities are mine).

Inference on estimates. There is no earnings gap for delivery to close: guidance sits on the floor, consensus sits on guidance, and my forecasts sit on consensus. I expect FY2027 consensus EPS to rise 1 to 2 percent over twelve months, from a slightly better FY2026 base, first-half strength and a buyback added net of interest. I expect FY2028 consensus EPS to end flat to slightly down once Medicare bidding is included. Sterling at about 1.32 dollars adds roughly 1.5 percent to EPS in pence.

Three things could make the upgrades larger: input inflation of 3 to 4 percent rather than a doubling; a deferral of Medicare bidding (plus 3.4 percent on FY2028 EPS); and a margin above the floor. One caution on the data: FactSet's revision counts are in reported dollars, so an organic upgrade offset by currency shows as no change, as it will for today's update.

Inference on the narrative: the larger scope lies here. Four changes arrive mechanically and will be visible on screens. Group organic growth including InnovaMatrix rises from about 4 percent in FY2026 to about 6.5 percent in FY2027. Reported EPS roughly doubles to about 21 cents as the $93m to $95m a year of spin-out amortisation, which ended in July 2026, drops out. The first half of 2027 shows the best year-on-year comparisons in years. And the FDA warning letter is expected to be lifted around the end of 2027. The story can move from "can they deliver the second half?" to "a mid-20s-margin grower outgrowing the market leader".
So what. The period from now to August 2027 is rich in dated, well-founded proofs with easy comparisons. The six months after August 2027 carry tougher comparisons and the Medicare decision. That sequence matters more for position sizing and timing than any single estimate.

The strongest counter-case. Every broker is already positive and targets are only 4 to 18 percent above the share price, so good news may simply be met with "valuation" notes. The first half of 2027 flatters the numbers; if the market looks through the first half to a second half growing EPS at 7 percent, the narrative stalls early.

What would change my view. An FY2026 margin of 23.2 percent or more, with an FY2027 floor above 24.0 percent, would be a true beat-and-raise and would move me to expect upgrades of 3 to 4 percent. A margin below the 23.0 percent floor would make every broker cut at once, by 2 to 4 percent.

Against the market. Brokers expect "modest upside to consensus", which matches my view. Brokers place the next buyback in February and count it gross of interest; I place it in August and count it net. No broker frames 2027 as two unequal halves.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is more likely restated than raised: the February FY2027 floor is about 1 in 10 to rise against 1 in 5 to fall, offset by about 3 in 10 that growth guidance is narrowed up in August; consensus FY2027 EPS is likely up only 1 to 2 percent, about 0.25 times 6.5 percent revenue growth (about the 55th percentile on the Universe illustration), with upside from inflation, a bidding deferral or a margin beat. The narrative, which counts least, has considerable and largely mechanical scope (organic growth from about 4 to 6.5 percent, reported EPS doubling, best comparisons in years, the FDA letter lifting), so slightly above the group's 52, above Spie and below Hexatronic.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Conclusion on #9The earnings case is simple and predictable within a narrow range. The risk lies in sudden payer or quality events, and in a share price whose near-term downside to a trough multiple exceeds its upside to the median multiple.

Simplicity. The case is simple by the standards of the sector. It has three drivers that barely depend on each other (Infusion-led growth, a margin bridge built on operating cost, and a buyback set by the leverage policy) and one dated binary event (Medicare bidding). Demand is non-discretionary.

The earnings cone. The range of EPS outcomes is narrow and roughly symmetric, widening only in FY2028 when the Medicare outcome enters: FY2027 EPS lies between minus 5 and plus 4 percent of the base case. The scenario weights are bear about 20 percent, base about 55 percent and bull about 25 percent. Today's comment on input inflation, if confirmed, tilts the 2027 range slightly upward.

The five judgements, step by step

1. The margin. FY2026 needs second-half operating profit of 587 less 262 = $325m. Each $10m of shortfall is 10 / 2,554 = 39 basis points of the full-year margin; after tax at 23 percent it is $7.7m of net income; over 1,966m shares that is 0.39 cents, or 1.9 percent of EPS. For FY2027, 50 basis points on revenue of $2,717m is $13.6m of operating profit (652 falls to 639); after tax at 24 percent it is $10.3m of net income (435 falls to 425); over 1,892m shares it is 0.55 cents, or 2.4 percent of EPS (23.0 falls to about 22.5 cents). The lower base carries into FY2028 at about 0.6 cents. Input inflation is the main route to a margin miss: each point above 3 percent costs $7m to $8m, or 1.3 percent of EPS; management's guide of 3 to 4 percent costs nil to 1.3 percent; a doubling of inflation would cost about 4 percent before mitigation.

2. Growth in 2027. One point of growth is 1 percent of $2,554m = $25.5m of revenue (2,717 falls to 2,692). At a 60 percent drop-through that is $15.3m of operating profit; after tax, $11.6m; over 1,892m shares, 0.61 cents, or 2.7 percent of EPS. The range is 1.7 percent (at the 38 percent incremental margin the company actually delivers) to 3.4 percent (at the full 75 percent contribution margin). For Infusion alone, each point of its growth is about $5.4m of revenue, 0.2 points of group growth and about 0.7 percent of EPS, so a five-point Infusion miss is about one point of group growth.

3. Medicare bidding in FY2028. The base case carries about $29m less revenue and $21m less operating profit than a world without bidding. If bidding is deferred: revenue rises from 2,880 to 2,909; operating profit from 701 to 722; net income is (722 less 86 of interest) x 0.76 = 483; EPS is 26.4 cents against an unrounded 25.55, plus 3.4 percent and above consensus. If bidding is harsh (Morgan Stanley's upper case of $60m of revenue at 90 percent drop-through, or $54m of operating profit): operating profit falls from 701 to 668; net income is 442; EPS is 24.2 cents, minus 5.5 percent. Weighted 30, 55 and 15 percent, the three outcomes give 25.6 cents, the base case.

4. Capital deployment. At about $3.60 a share, $225m retires 62m shares, 3.4 percent of the FY2028 share count. Without the buyback, FY2028 EPS is 3.3 percent lower before interest; the interest saved ($225m x 5.2 percent x 0.76 = $8.9m) gives back 1.9 percent; the net effect is minus 1.4 percent. No buybacks for three years would leave FY2029 EPS about 4 percent lower (29.0 falls to about 27.8 cents). If the cash goes to an acquisition instead, EPS may be similar but the risk is not: Convatec's acquisition record includes one large write-off.

5. Sterling. FY2027 EPS of 23.0 cents is 17.4p at 1.32 dollars to the pound and 16.5p at 1.39, a fall of 5 percent with nothing changed in the business. At 14.2 times, that fall is worth about 13p on the share price. Convatec's currency hedges run only 12 months.

Tails outside the cone (each of low probability). An escalation of FDA action at Reynosa, the one physical site that sits under both the growth driver and the margin driver; a new CMS action; a product recall (the October 2026 ESENTA recall came from a contract manufacturing site); a pump partner bringing infusion sets in-house, or the market moving faster to tubeless pumps.

Suddenness, trackability and precedent. Demand risk is slow and can be tracked through partners' results; payer and quality risks are sudden.

Convatec's own history shows the scale of sudden risks. Two profit warnings in 2017 and 2018, caused by plant transfers, took the multiple from 19 to 10.5 times. A Medicare proposal in July 2025 took the multiple from 18.8 to 14.6 times in one month, a 19 percent fall in the share price, before anything had changed in earnings. An FDA warning letter in early 2026 cost 10 percent of the share price within a day.

Across the sector, the lasting de-ratings came from payer resets (skin substitutes), quality failures (Philips Respironics) and dilutive acquisitions (Coloplast's Atos and Kerecis), never from demand. Convatec carries no cyclicality risk in the ordinary sense; the cycle that matters is the sector's valuation wave, which follows bond yields.

The share-price cone is wider and more skewed than the earnings cone. On unchanged forward earnings, 11 times is about 207p (minus 23 percent), and the five-year median of 16.55 times is about 312p (plus 16 percent). At 10.5 times with a 5 to 8 percent earnings miss, the price is 182p to 188p, and brokers' published bear cases are 160p to 166p. In the first few months the downside step is larger than the upside step; time repairs that imbalance as earnings grow (#12).

The strongest counter-case. This analysis may understate the risk. The forecast is more concentrated than the diffuse past record that makes it credible, and with every broker positive, a miss would be cut by all of them at once. Against that, today's update removed the largest near-term risk, the second-half revenue step.

What would change my view. Upward: the FY2026 margin printed, the hedge cover disclosed and the payment amounts published; each removes a named risk. Downward: any adverse event at Reynosa.

Against the market. The market describes Convatec's risk as execution. After today I would describe the risk as concentration and price paid: one franchise (Infusion), one plant (Reynosa), one binary event (Medicare bidding) and a multiple that has moved 22 percent ahead of estimates.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. The earnings case is simple and narrow: three largely independent drivers, non-discretionary demand and an FY2027 EPS cone of minus 5 to plus 4 percent, with each named judgement worth 1.4 to 5.5 percent of EPS. Held in the low 60s by sudden, partly binary risks that the share price has repeatedly amplified (a Medicare proposal took 19 percent off the price in a month, an FDA letter 10 percent in a day), a single FDA-flagged plant under both the growth and margin legs, leverage of about 2.1 times (worse than about two-thirds of the Universe) and a price cone wider than the earnings cone; between the groups' 50 and 64, just below OEM International and above Banca Generali.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion on #10The stock is turning up and entering thesis broadening. Broadening is likely to peak around the August 2027 results, and the Medicare payment amounts in late summer 2027 will decide the next phase.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places Convatec in the Turning/Inflecting phase. The sequence of worries since the low supports that placing and suggests that the next phase, broadening, is opening:

The multiple has retraced about 37 percent of its fall from 18.8 times (June 2025) to 11.5 times (May 2026). Dollar estimates have not yet turned up. Technical momentum is recovering from a flat base.

Inference. Convatec is not yet in the reinforcing phase, because that phase needs rising estimates and there are none yet. Convatec's own history shows how fast a turn can run once a worry clears: the multiple went from 10.5 times in December 2018 to 18.2 times in October 2019, in ten months, on a new chief executive and a plan, before the numbers had improved. The multiple then traded mostly between 16 and 21 times for more than four years while the company delivered.

So what. Broadening most likely builds through the February 2027 results and peaks around the August 2027 results. The following six months risk looking like a stall, for reasons of comparison and Medicare timing, not because of the business. If Medicare bidding is deferred or mild, the stock can move to the reinforcing phase in late 2027; if bidding is harsh, the stock returns to the turning phase.

The strongest counter-case. The 2019 re-rating rode a sector whose multiples were rising as bond yields fell. Today the worry that matters most is external, so management cannot clear it by executing. And a share that has risen 23 percent in ten weeks on unchanged estimates may already be discounting the broadening.

What would change my view. A margin miss on 23 Feb 2027 would put the stock back into the bottoming phase. A beat-and-raise on that date would confirm broadening.

Against the market. My view is in line with brokers' "re-rating under way". I am more specific about when the re-rating is most vulnerable: the six months after August 2027.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. The memo's Turning Up at the threshold of Broadening is right and the computed Bottoming lags: three worries have cleared, the first near-term guidance raise under the new chief executive came today, the acceleration is now visible and a dated run of easy comparisons and proofs runs to August 2027. Held off the top because dollar estimates have not yet turned up (3-month revision 3 percent, 70th percentile; 6-month 56th), the price has risen 23 percent on flat estimates, and the largest worry, Medicare payment amounts, is external and late in the window; close to Reply's Turning short of Broadening, above Kerry's mid-cycle Reinforcing.

#11The fair multiple

Conclusion on #11The guideline of 17.34 times is a fair multiple for Convatec delivering without its overhangs, and a reasonable three-year destination. For the end of 2027, I regard about 16 times as the central case and 17.34 times as the favourable case.

The guideline. The guideline fair multiple is 17.34 times two-year-forward earnings: the 60th percentile of the stock's ten-year history, as set for the Turning/Inflecting phase. The guideline is 22 percent above today's 14.2 times. The model summary applies 19.27 times instead, which on my interpolation sits near the 80th percentile of ten years and above the five-year 90th percentile (18.88 times); end note A3 records the discrepancy. My view below is of 17.34 times.

Evidence.

  • Own history. The ten-year percentiles of the two-year-forward P/E are: 10th 13.2 times, 35th 15.5, median 16.6 and 75th 18.7. Today's 14.2 times is at about the 20th percentile on my interpolation. The stock traded at or above 17 times in most months from late 2019 to early 2024, and at 18.8 times as recently as June 2025.
  • What took the multiple down. Six worries took the multiple down: Medicare bidding, InnovaMatrix, a chief executive's death, the second-half growth step, the FDA warning letter and a sector de-rating. Three of the six have cleared.
  • What brokers apply. Morgan Stanley applies 15 times 2028 earnings; Jefferies 14 to 15 times 2027 earnings; Bernstein 17 times, blended with a cash-flow valuation; DNB Carnegie 18 times. Brokers' bull cases use 18 to 22 times, and their bear cases 10 to 12 times.
  • Relative. Coloplast trades at about 18 times. At 17.34 times, Convatec would trade roughly level with the market leader.
  • Sector share. About a fifth of the daily variance in Convatec's share price, and about half of its six-month move, have been shared with peers.

My view. 17.34 times fairly describes what Convatec is worth when it is delivering and unencumbered. The guideline sits just above the median of a decade in which the business was weaker than it is now, and the stock has made this journey before.

As a 13-month destination, however, 17.34 times is the upper part of the plausible range, not the centre. To reach 17.34 times by the end of 2027, the multiple must retrace about 80 percent of its fall, which needs a clean margin print, a benign Medicare bidding outcome and a sector that keeps recovering, all together. My central expectation for the end of 2027 is about 16 times, in a range of 14.5 to 17.5 times, with roughly a one-in-three chance of 17.34 times or more.

As a three-year destination, once bidding is known and absorbed and the mid-20s margin is banked, the guideline looks right and possibly conservative.

So what. Use the guideline with a time stamp: fair for mid-2029, generous for December 2027. Each turn of the multiple is worth about 7 percent of the share price, so the difference between 16 and 17.34 times is about 8 percent of return.

The strongest counter-case, both ways. Lower: at 6 to 8 percent growth, mid-teens returns on capital and no pricing power, Convatec may deserve only 15 times in a world of 5 percent bond yields, which is the multiple the two brokers closest to the company apply; and a multiple above Coloplast's would be a first for Convatec. Higher: EPS growing 13 to 14 percent, against Coloplast's 9 percent, justifies parity or more, and 18 to 19 times was normal for Convatec when it delivered less.

What would change my view. Upward: Medicare bidding deferred, or payment amounts implying a cut near 20 percent, together with a margin above the floor. Downward: a sector de-rating on bond yields, or a margin miss, either of which would make 14 to 15 times the ceiling for a year.

Against the market. The guideline sits at the top of the range of multiples brokers apply. My central view of 16 times sits between the multiples most brokers apply and the guideline.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Cheap on own history; on the memo's single-peer comparison Convatec is dearer than normal against Coloplast, which by rule would give C, but that narrowing is deserved because Convatec's EPS now grows 13 to 15 percent against Coloplast's 1 to 9 and the gap is closing from both ends, so I read the peer measure as neutral and give B. Placed at the floor of the band because after today's rise the own-range reading sits at the cheap boundary, part of the cheapness is deserved by the open payer overhang, and the peer reading rests on one company.

#12Total shareholder return

Conclusion on #12At the guideline multiple the total return is about 42 percent to the end of 2027 and about 24 percent a year to mid-2029. Re-rating drives the return first, then 13 to 14 percent earnings growth increasingly takes over, and the three-year downside is close to nil even at a trough multiple.

Status of the figures. The return arithmetic below is mine, by hand, because the model's own return at the guideline multiple rests on its faulty share count (end note A2). The arithmetic uses the model's net income, the Analyst's share-count path and the guideline multiple, at a constant exchange rate of 1.34 dollars to the pound. At today's rate of about 1.32, every pence value is about 1.5 percent higher.

To 31 Dec 2027 (13 months from today; the model's 18-month column)

  • Forward EPS today is 18.83p (about 25.2 cents). Forward EPS at the end of 2027 is FY2029's: 29.0 cents, or 21.6p. The earnings leg is therefore plus 15 percent.
  • The multiple leg at the guideline is 17.34 / 14.2 = plus 22 percent.
  • Price: 21.6p x 17.34 = 375p, plus 40 percent (1.15 x 1.22).
  • Dividends of about 8.5 cents (the FY2026 final and FY2027 interim dividends), or about 6p, add 2.4 percent. The model counts 4.5 percent because its column starts on 30 Jun 2026.
  • Total: about plus 42 percent, about half of it from the multiple.

To 30 Jun 2029 (2.6 years; the model's three-year column)

Forward EPS at mid-2029 spans the second half of FY2030 and the first half of FY2031. The model stops at FY2030 (33.0 cents); assuming FY2031 EPS grows 12.5 percent, forward EPS is about 35 cents, or 26.2p. That forward EPS rests on years to which I give low weight.

  • Earnings leg plus 39 percent; multiple leg at the guideline plus 22 percent; price 454p, plus 69 percent; dividends of about 19p, plus 7 percent (the model has 7.6 percent).
  • Total: about plus 76 percent, or about 24 percent a year, with earnings supplying more than half.

The nearer view, six months. By mid-May 2027 forward EPS has rolled up about 7 percent. At an unchanged multiple the return is about plus 7 to plus 8 percent; at 16 times it is about plus 20 percent; and at 12.5 times after a margin miss it is about minus 6 percent.

What drives the return.

  1. Earnings growth of 13 to 14 percent a year, of which about 6 points come from revenue, 2.5 from margin and 4 from the falling share count. The earnings leg is the reliable one and is worth about 15 percent to the end of 2027.
  2. The multiple, worth about 22 percent if the guideline is reached. The multiple leg depends on the worry stack in #10 and partly on the sector.
  3. Dividends and buybacks: a dividend yield of about 2.3 percent, plus buybacks already counted in EPS. Together, dividends and buybacks return about 5.5 percent of Convatec's market value a year.
Inference: the skew. Over 13 months the range of returns is wide, and the central outcome (about plus 30 percent at 16 times) rests half on re-rating. Over three years the distribution shifts right and narrows: the unchanged-multiple case earns about 16 percent a year, and the trough-with-a-miss case is about nil. The asymmetry Richard looks for is therefore stronger over three years than over one, and it comes from compounding, not from estimate upgrades.

The strongest counter-case. The return starts from a price that has risen 23 percent since September on unchanged estimates, so some of the multiple leg has already been spent. A 13-month horizon ends just after the Medicare decision and during the weaker half of 2027, which is the least favourable moment to measure. The three-year arithmetic leans on FY2030 and FY2031 EPS.

What would change my view. The repaired model, if its share-count path differs from the Analyst's (a flat buyback price would lift FY2030 EPS by about 2 percent); a different FY2029 EPS; the sterling exchange rate.

Against the market. Brokers' targets imply returns of 4 to 18 percent over twelve months, on 14.5 to 18 times. My central 13-month return is higher because I roll earnings forward to FY2029, and most brokers do not.

Score: 82, set by the Rater. About +28 to +30 percent sits in the 20 to 35 percent B band, about 83 to 85 on the scale, with a supportive three-year check (+46 percent, about 16 percent a year, even at an unchanged multiple, and about nil at a trough with a miss). Placed down to 82 because about half the 13-month return is re-rating and the near-term lower tail is fatter than the upper (the downside step to a trough multiple exceeds the upside to the median, and the window ends just after the Medicare decision).

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Convatec is an above-average, non-cyclical consumables business with two genuine moats, a management team that does what it says, and an earnings path of 13 to 14 percent a year that is reliable to 2027 and plausible to 2030. Today Convatec showed the growth it had promised, and it quietly showed more margin strength than the headline admits.

The investment case is not an upgrade story. Guidance, consensus and my forecasts sit on the same line, so delivery alone moves estimates by a percent or two. The case is a story of worries clearing in sequence, on top of dependable compounding, at a multiple still in the bottom quarter of its ten-year range. Three worries are gone. The two that remain and matter are the margin print on 23 Feb 2027 and the Medicare payment amounts in late summer 2027.

The calendar favours the next nine months: an easy first half of 2027, a likely buyback in August and mechanical improvements in the reported numbers. The second half of 2027 is tougher on comparisons and carries the Medicare binary. The earnings risk is low and well mapped; the share-price risk is higher, because the multiple has moved first, and about half of that move came with the sector.

The most useful single observation for the decision is about time. Over one year the outcome depends mostly on the multiple, and the range of outcomes is wide. Over three years the outcome depends mostly on earnings, and the range is favourable from top to bottom.

Set by the Rater. Concentrated, sticky oligopolies, non-discretionary recurring demand, churn under 1 percent and steadily rising margins make the franchise more robust than its ordinary returns suggest (topic 3 at 63), and a constant-currency record of beating and raising margin floors (topic 4 at 68) supports it; in Richard's CVS sense stability lifts it above topic 3, but it stays below the 75 band because there is no pricing power, the structure is fragile against the payer, Convatec is a challenger in its largest markets and acquisitions have destroyed value.
Setups' Fit/Crispness75
Set by the Rater. The case fits 'Major CfC Clearing in MQ non-cyclical or better business on Q1 multiple, leading to reversion to normal' in substance: a non-cyclical, above-average business on a bottom-quartile multiple with a dated stack of worries, three already cleared and two dated; I disregard the memo's point that the multiple has already moved, which belongs to timing and price, and hold it at 75 rather than higher because current problems (the FDA letter at the Infusion plant, a leadership bench in transition, cash lagging earnings) blur the fit.
Case Riskiness66
Set by the Rater. Over topic 9 at 63: the earnings case is boring and narrow with mostly paper-cut risks, management guides conservatively and the multiple is low in its range, which in Richard's CVS sense lifts it a little above topic 9; but a dated payer binary with a precedent of sudden de-rating, one FDA-flagged plant under both growth and margin, leverage of about 2.1 times and a price that has run ahead of estimates keep it out of the 75 band.

End notes A: the numbers behind the memo

A1Price. The dashboard's last price is 252.8p (16 Nov 2026). The shares rose about 9 percent on today's update, to about 268p (press reports cited in the research answers; the AlphaSense report of brokers' notes confirms the size of the move). The memo uses 268p. At 268p the two-year-forward P/E is about 14.2 times on the dashboard's forward EPS of 18.83p.
A2The model. The Financial Analyst's model (update 2) is sound from revenue down to net income, but its share count is faulty, and the request to repair the share count is still open. The model summary's EPS line (which starts at minus 3.79), its net debt path and its return at the guideline multiple (minus 1,236 percent) are artefacts of that fault, and the memo does not use them. EPS in this memo is the model's net income divided by the Analyst's share-count path, which is the model's own cross-check. The return arithmetic in #12 is mine, by hand, and should be replaced by the model's once the model is repaired.
A3The guideline fair multiple. The Phases data gives 17.34 times (the 60th percentile of ten years, for a stock in the Turning/Inflecting phase); the model summary applies 19.27 times. The memo treats 17.34 times as the guideline and shows 19.27 times beside it; the two files disagree and should be reconciled. The Phases data was struck before today's update and shows a current multiple of 13.94 times and a 24 percent gap to the guideline.
A4Evidence dated after today's update. Evidence dated after the update comes from one AlphaSense report that summarises the results call and the notes of four brokers (Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank, Jefferies and Bernstein). I rate the report medium confidence; one figure in it does not reconcile (the Morgan Stanley segment growth rates discussed in #2).
A5The Earnings Review. I checked the caution in the brief. The latest Earnings Review covers the interim results for the six months to 30 Jun 2026, published on 4 Aug 2026, and states that no later results exist. Today's update is covered by the research answers and the AlphaSense report.
A6Forecast inputs. I have changed no forecast inputs. After update 2 the model's inputs match my view in every year, so there is no inputs-changed.md file.

End notes B: the visuals and abbreviations

  • Charts marked as drawn take their figures from the memo; where a figure is derived (the second half of 2027 in #6, the FY2028 range in #9), the note under the chart says so.
  • Three charts were added in editing: the buyback effect gross and net of interest (#5), equity free cash flow against buybacks (#6) and the total return by horizon (#12). Each takes its figures from the memo's own tables and arithmetic.
  • Three default visuals are left out because they rest on the model's faulty share count (end note A2): the financial trajectory chart (its Viewforth EPS line starts at minus 3.79), the line-by-line comparison of Viewforth with consensus (its EPS row shows the same artefact) and the total shareholder return chart (minus 1,236 percent at 19.27 times). The returns in #12 are the Analyst's hand arithmetic instead.
  • The valuation chart in #10 covers five years; its bands are the ten-year percentiles. The chart was struck before today's rise.
  • Default visuals come from FactSet, the Master Dashboard and the Financial Analyst's model (update 2), as listed with each chart.
  • Abbreviations: bp, basis points; CMS, the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services; FDA, the US Food and Drug Administration; H1 and H2, the first and second halves of a financial year; ROIC, return on invested capital; x, times (as in a P/E multiple).

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
